analysis:
This batch contains only documentation changes: a new changelog fragment (changelog.d/installer-release-file-modes.md, lines 1-3) and a docs/operations/provider-release.md edit (head lines 411-414) plus a date bump on line 3. The text states that the installer extracts the release bundle with /usr/bin/tar under umask 022, so a restrictive caller umask does not leave installed app files owner-only. Private state created elsewhere keeps its own modes. The actual scripts/install.sh change (install_bundle_atomically) is not in this batch, so I could not verify it.

Security relevance by threat model: the change relates to TB-003 (operator vs process) and the installer's signature and hash verification, but the text does not alter the verification flow. The doc says the bin/ hash checks, the staged app signature verification (verify_staged_app_signature) and the production Apple-team requirement are unchanged. Using the absolute path /usr/bin/tar reduces the risk of PATH hijacking of tar. umask 022 makes installed app files world-readable. That is expected for a signed, public, notarized app bundle and exposes no secrets (A-001, A-003 and A-008 are unaffected). The doc explicitly says private state keeps restrictive modes. The remaining integration question is whether the umask 022 scope in install.sh is subshell-limited. If it leaked to later steps, it could loosen modes on provider.toml, tokens or key material (A-008). That is outside the supplied evidence, so I record it as an unverified contract. The next pass should check scripts/install.sh for the umask scoping, a restored umask, and the modes of the config and token files created after extraction.

No trust-boundary, attestation, authorization or encryption behavior changes appear in the supplied files, and no findings qualify.
